Complex phases and oscillatory distributions

Exposition and original illustrations by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI). Public domain (CC0 1.0).

An integral can define a distribution even when its amplitude grows at infinity. Cancellation must then compensate for two different effects: frequency derivatives improve the amplitude, whereas derivatives in the observed variable may enlarge it. A nonnegative imaginary part supplies additional decay without changing this balance. We construct the distribution, locate its possible singularities and their covector directions, and determine the exact normalization of the wave propagator.

The analytic input is Weighted cancellation for complex phases, Theorem 1 and Corollary 4, including the proof of its uniform estimate (W20). Schwartz functions and Fourier inversion, F1–F5, proves all Fourier operations used below. Convolution as addition of supports, B0–B2 and Theorem 1.1, supplies distributional gluing, parameter pairings and proper convolution. The causal fundamental distribution used in the last theorem is constructed in Causal point sources and characteristic cones, Lemma 4.0 and formulas (4.0g)–(4.0h). Integration, compact cutoffs and differentiation under dominated integrals are proved in the integration foundations, §§15.0–15.4, and the scalar foundations, §§13.1–13.5 and 13.10.

This estimate makes the definition independent of the choice of a smaller cutoff, and makes the regular set open and positively conic. Finally, Indeed, if every direction over is regular, compactness of the unit sphere supplies finitely many smaller regular cones covering it. Proof. The power series and all its derivatives converge on compact sets, proving smoothness at zero. Away from zero, each time derivative is a sine or cosine times a power of ; on a compact time interval it has polynomial growth, uniformly in time. For the zeroth derivative use the bound . Schwartz decay therefore justifies differentiating the test pairing any number of times, uniformly on bounded Schwartz families. The Fourier identities in F2–F5 give the differential equation from the elementary multiplier equation . They give and .

Choose a smooth cutoff near . The high-frequency part is the difference of the two oscillatory integrals The high-frequency amplitudes have order and type . Both phases are real, degree one in , and have nonzero joint gradient since their -gradient is . The cutoff limits agree with (O20): after pairing first in , rapid decrease of the transformed compact test gives absolute convergence, uniformly for in its compact support. The low-frequency part is smooth in . The frequency gradients of the two phases are Their possible zeros project into ; Theorem 3 proves the singular-support inclusion in (O21).

The products in (O22) are defined by integrating the smooth distribution-valued function over the indicated time half-line against a compact test. To justify time integration by parts, pair with its smooth, compactly supported spatial test depending on ; the Fourier estimates above and the parameter pairing proof B1 justify the product rule. Two integrations by parts give Thus . Since is odd in , time reflection gives the negative-half-line formula and the same unit point source. Also almost everywhere in the defining time integral, proving the difference formula in (O22).
